questions.answer: We need an antiderivative of \(5x^4\). Use the power rule for antiderivatives: \(\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\) for \(n\ne-1\). Thus \(\int 5x^4\,dx=5\cdot\frac{x^5}{5}+C=x^5+C\). Differentiating \(x^5+C\) gives \(5x^4\), so the final answer is \(x^5+C\).

We need the general antiderivative. Integrate term by term using linearity. \(\int6x^2\,dx=6\cdot\frac{x^3}{3}=2x^3\), \(\int(-4x)\,dx=-4\cdot\frac{x^2}{2}=-2x^2\), and \(\int9\,dx=9x\). Include the constant of integration. Therefore \(\int(6x^2-4x+9)\,dx=2x^3-2x^2+9x+C\).

We need to rewrite powers before integrating. Since \(\frac{3}{x^2}=3x^{-2}\) and \(2\sqrt{x}=2x^{1/2}\), the integral is \(\int(3x^{-2}+2x^{1/2})\,dx\). Apply the power rule: \(\int3x^{-2}\,dx=3\cdot\frac{x^{-1}}{-1}=-3x^{-1}\), and \(\int2x^{1/2}\,dx=2\cdot\frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2}=\frac{4}{3}x^{3/2}\). Therefore the antiderivative is \(-\frac{3}{x}+\frac{4}{3}x^{3/2}+C\).

We need an antiderivative of each term. The antiderivative of \(e^x\) is \(e^x\), because \(\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x\). The antiderivative of \(\cos x\) is \(\sin x\), because \(\frac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x\). Therefore \(\int(e^x+\cos x)\,dx=e^x+\sin x+C\).

We need standard antiderivatives. Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x\), \(\int\sec^2 x\,dx=\tan x\). For \(x>0\), \(\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx=\ln x\). Combining the terms and adding the constant gives \(\tan x+\ln x+C\).

We need the specific antiderivative satisfying the initial condition. Integrate \(f'(x)\): \(f(x)=\int(4x^3-6x)\,dx=x^4-3x^2+C\). Use \(f(1)=5\): \(1^4-3(1)^2+C=5\), so \(1-3+C=5\), giving \(C=7\). Therefore \(f(x)=x^4-3x^2+7\).

We need the function \(y(x)\). Rewrite \(3\sqrt{x}\) as \(3x^{1/2}\). Integrate: \(y=\int3x^{1/2}\,dx=3\cdot\frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2}+C=2x^{3/2}+C\). Use the condition \(y=10\) when \(x=4\): \(10=2(4^{3/2})+C\). Since \(4^{3/2}=8\), \(10=16+C\), so \(C=-6\). Therefore \(y=2x^{3/2}-6\).

We need to handle the special \(x^{-1}\) term separately. For \(2x^{-3}\), the power rule gives \(2\cdot\frac{x^{-2}}{-2}=-x^{-2}\). For \(-7x^{-1}\), use \(\int x^{-1}\,dx=\ln x\) because \(x>0\). Thus the antiderivative is \(-x^{-2}-7\ln x+C\), or \(-\frac{1}{x^2}-7\ln x+C\).

questions.prompt: Verify that \(F(x)=\frac{x^5}{5}-2x^2+8\) is an antiderivative of \(f(x)=x^4-4x\).
questions.answer: We need to check whether \(F'(x)=f(x)\). Differentiate term by term: \(\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x^5}{5}=x^4\), \(\frac{d}{dx}(-2x^2)=-4x\), and \(\frac{d}{dx}8=0\). Therefore \(F'(x)=x^4-4x\), which equals \(f(x)\). Hence \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\).

questions.prompt: Find the position function \(s(t)\) if velocity \(v(t)=6t-4\) m/s and \(s(0)=3\) m.
questions.answer: We need position from velocity, so integrate \(v(t)\). Since \(s'(t)=v(t)=6t-4\), \(s(t)=\int(6t-4)\,dt=3t^2-4t+C\). Use \(s(0)=3\): \(3(0)^2-4(0)+C=3\), so \(C=3\). Therefore \(s(t)=3t^2-4t+3\) m.
